app.name: Banas Radar
app.description: See which parts of the Philippines have dangerous heat right now and stay safe.

tip.safe: Nice weather! Still, bring water if you'll be out long.
tip.caution: Medyo mainit. Drink water often and take breaks in the shade.
tip.extremeCaution: Grabe ang banas! Limit time outside from 10 AM to 4 PM and keep hydrated.
tip.danger: Delikado na. Stay indoors muna, check on seniors and kids, and watch for heat exhaustion.
tip.extremeDanger: Heat stroke is likely. Avoid going outside. If someone feels dizzy or confused, call 911.

vulnerable.title: Heat safety for you
vulnerable.description: Get stricter heat advice if you are a senior, caring for kids, pregnant, or work outdoors.
vulnerable.heading: Who should we watch out for?
vulnerable.body: PAGASA colors stay the same. We just treat the heat as more dangerous for you — earlier rest, more water, cooler places.
vulnerable.bannerBody: We treat today's heat as hotter for {groups}.
vulnerable.shiftNote: We add {degrees}°C when we classify heat for your group.

groupBody.senior: Age 60+ — overheat faster, and heat can raise blood pressure or confuse thinking.
groupBody.child: Young kids and babies. Shade, water, and rest every 20 minutes.
groupBody.pregnant: Buntis? Extra fluid, avoid 10 AM–4 PM sun, rest at the first dizzy spell.
groupBody.outdoorWorker: Riders, vendors, construction. 15-min shade break every hour, ice water, wet cloth on the neck.

extra.senior: Seniors: stay in aircon if you can, sip water even if you're not thirsty, and text family you're okay.
extra.child: Kids overheat faster. Shade, water, no long noon play, and never leave anyone in a parked vehicle.
extra.pregnant: Buntis: extra fluid, loose clothes, and sit down at the first dizzy or cramp.
extra.outdoorWorker: Riders at vendors: park in shade, 15-min break every hour, ice water, wet cloth on neck and wrists.

firstAid.title: Heat first aid
firstAid.description: Tick the signs you see. We'll name heat stroke, exhaustion, cramps, and more — and tell you what to do, including when to call 911.
firstAid.heading: Heat first aid
firstAid.body: Tick every sign you see. We'll name the likely condition and what to do. This is first aid, not a hospital. When in doubt, tumawag sa 911.
firstAid.checkHint: Check all that apply. One sign is enough to start.
firstAid.checkEmpty: Tick at least one sign to see the likely condition.
firstAid.call911Hint: Works even if you're offline. Stay on the line until help says you can hang up.

redFlags.one: Confused, slurred speech, seizure, or hindi nagigising
redFlags.two: Very hot skin, stopped sweating, or breathing is hard
redFlags.three: Vomiting and cannot keep water down
redFlags.four: A baby, senior, or buntis is getting worse fast

firstAid.disclaimer: Not a substitute for a doctor. PAGASA heat categories tell you the risk; this page tells you what to do.

symptoms.confused: Confused, slurred speech, or won't wake up
symptoms.hotSkin: Skin is very hot — dry or still sweating
symptoms.heavySweat: Heavy sweat, cold or clammy skin
symptoms.dizzy: Dizzy, weak, or a bad headache
symptoms.cramps: Painful muscle cramps in legs, arms, or belly
symptoms.thirst: Very thirsty, dry mouth, or dark urine

heatStroke.title: Heat stroke
heatStroke.summary: The body cannot cool down. This can kill. Call 911 first, then cool the person.

signs.two: Very hot skin — dry, or still sweating
signs.three: Fast pulse, throbbing headache, or slurred speech
signs.four: They may deny they are sick

do.one: Call 911. Cool them while you wait.
do.two: Move to shade or aircon. Take off extra clothes.
do.three: Wet the skin, fan hard, ice packs on neck, armpits, and groin.
do.four: If they are awake and can swallow, small sips of water only.

dont.one: Don’t give food or drinks if they are confused or unconscious.
dont.three: Don’t use paracetamol or ibuprofen to “bring the fever down.” Cool the body instead.

heatExhaustion.title: Heat exhaustion
heatExhaustion.summary: The body is overheating but still fighting. Treat it now so it does not become heat stroke.

signs.one: Heavy sweat, cold or clammy skin
signs.four: They can still talk and know where they are

do.one: Stop work. Move to shade or aircon.
do.two: Loosen clothes. Lie down, elevate the legs.
do.three: Sip cool water or oral rehydration every few minutes.
do.four: Wet cloth on neck and wrists. Rest at least 30 minutes.

dont.one: Don’t send them back to the sun or the road until they feel normal.
dont.two: Don’t give alcohol, energy drinks, or coffee as the only fluid.
dont.three: If no improvement in 30 minutes, or they vomit or get confused — treat as heat stroke and call 911.

heatCramps.title: Heat cramps
heatCramps.summary: Painful muscle spasms after hard work or long rides in the heat — often legs, arms, or belly.

signs.one: Sudden tight, painful spasms during or after work
signs.two: Sweating a lot, muscles feel hard

do.one: Stop the activity. Rest in a cool place.
do.two: Sip water or oral rehydration. Don’t chug.
do.three: Gently stretch and hold the muscle. Light massage is okay.

dont.two: Don’t go back to heavy work the same hour. Cramp plus more heat can become exhaustion.

dehydration.title: Dehydration
dehydration.summary: Not enough water. Common for riders, vendors, and anyone who waits until they are very thirsty.

signs.two: Dark yellow urine, or wala pang ihi for hours

do.one: Sit in shade. Sip water often — small and steady.
do.two: Use oral rehydration if dizzy or after heavy sweat.
do.three: Eat a little (banana, soup, rice) once they can keep fluids down.

dont.one: Don’t wait for extreme thirst. That’s already late.
dont.two: Don’t use soda or alcohol to rehydrate.

heatSyncope.title: Heat fainting
heatSyncope.summary: Biglaang hilo or nahimatay after standing long in the sun — blood pools in the legs.

signs.one: Sudden dizziness, tunnel vision, then collapse
signs.three: Usually wakes up after lying down

do.one: Lay them flat. Elevate the legs. Cool place.
do.two: Loosen tight clothes. Fan and wet cloth.
do.three: When fully awake, sip water. Stay down for several minutes.

dont.one: Don’t sit them up fast or make them walk it off.
dont.two: Don’t give food or drink until they are fully awake.
dont.three: Call 911 if they don’t wake in one minute, hit their head, have a seizure, or stay confused.

heatRash.title: Heat rash (bungang-araw)
heatRash.summary: Tiny itchy bumps when sweat is trapped under clothes. Uncomfortable, usually not an emergency.

signs.one: Small red or clear bumps, prickly itch
signs.two: Often under the shirt, neck, or skin folds
signs.three: Worse in noon heat and tight clothes

do.one: Move to a cooler, drier place. Loose cotton clothes.
do.two: Wash gently, pat dry. Let skin breathe.
do.three: If very itchy, a doctor can suggest a light cream. Watch for infection.

dont.one: Don’t use thick ointment or oil that blocks sweat.
dont.two: Don’t scratch until it bleeds. If it gets pus, fever, or spreads fast, see a clinic.
